title: Storm Damage and Roof Insurance Claims in AZ | Integrity Roofing
desc: What to do after a monsoon damages your Arizona roof: document safely, call your insurer, prepare for the adjuster, protect the home and avoid storm chasers.
h1: Storm damage and roof insurance claims in Arizona
lead: A monsoon can lift tiles, tear shingles and drive rain under a roof in minutes. This guide walks through what to do in the hours and weeks after a storm, from safe photos to the adjuster visit.
answer: After storm damage, stay off the roof, photograph what you can see from the ground and inside, and limit further water damage with buckets and tarps on belongings. Call your insurance company to report the loss and ask how they handle roof claims, then have a licensed Arizona roofer inspect and document the damage. This guide is general information, not legal or insurance advice; your policy and your insurer decide what is covered.

sections.h2: First, a note on what this guide is
sections.body:
Every insurance policy is different, and only your insurer can tell you what your policy covers, what your deductible is and how their claim process works. This guide shares general guidance we have learned from years of repairing storm-damaged roofs in the Valley. It is not legal or insurance advice.

If you have questions about your rights as a policyholder, the Arizona Department of Insurance and Financial Institutions has consumer resources, and a licensed insurance agent or attorney can answer questions about your specific situation.

sections.h2: Stay safe right after the storm
sections.body:
Monsoon season in Arizona runs June 15–September 30, and the worst storms often bring high wind, dust, lightning and sudden heavy rain. Wait until the storm has fully passed before you go outside. Watch for downed power lines, broken branches hanging in trees and loose tiles or debris that could still fall from the roof edge.

Do not climb onto the roof. Wet tile, loose granules and storm debris make roofs slick, and a damaged deck may not hold your weight. A fall from a single-story roof can cause serious injury. Everything you need to document can be done from the ground and from inside the house.

sections.h2: Document the damage from the ground and inside
sections.body: Good records make the rest of the process easier. Start as soon as it is safe and keep everything in one folder on your phone or computer.
bullets: Take wide photos of each side of the house, then closer shots of any damage you can see from the yard.
Photograph tiles, shingle pieces or flashing that landed in the yard before you move them, then set them aside.
Use binoculars or your phone's zoom to capture missing tiles, lifted shingles, bent drip edge or torn coating.
Inside, photograph ceiling stains, drips, wet insulation in the attic and any damaged belongings.
Write down the date and approximate time of the storm and anything you noticed, such as a loud bang or when the leak started.
Keep receipts for buckets, tarps, fans, a hotel stay or anything else you buy because of the damage.

sections.h2: Prevent more damage while you wait
sections.body:
Most homeowner policies expect you to take reasonable steps to keep damage from getting worse. Inside the house, that can mean moving furniture and electronics, catching drips in buckets, laying towels down and running fans. If a ceiling is bulging with water, keep people away from it and call a professional; do not poke it while standing under it.

On the roof itself, temporary protection such as a tarp is best done by a roofer. Tarping a tile roof is tricky because walking on tile breaks it and a tarp that is weighted or nailed the wrong way can cause new leaks. Call us at 602-548-3770 to schedule an inspection. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

Report the loss to your insurer as soon as you reasonably can. Many policies have time limits for reporting damage, so do not wait weeks to see if the leak goes away. When you call, have your policy number, the date of the storm and your photos ready.

Ask questions and write down the answers, along with the name of each person you speak with:
bullets: Is the claim number assigned, and who is my adjuster?
What is my deductible for wind or storm damage?
Will an adjuster inspect the roof in person, and how soon?
Do you want a roofer's inspection report or repair estimate before the adjuster visit?
Are temporary repairs covered, and what documentation do you need for them?

sections.h2: What to expect at the adjuster visit
sections.body:
The adjuster works for the insurance company and is there to look at the damage and decide what the policy covers. Many adjusters will walk the roof, measure it and photograph damaged areas. Some homeowners like to have their roofer present so both people are looking at the same tiles, shingles and flashing at the same time.

Share your photos, your timeline and your roofer's report. Afterward, the insurer will usually send a written estimate or a letter explaining their decision. Read it closely. If something seems missing, such as underlayment damage the adjuster did not see, ask your insurer how to request a review and provide any supporting documentation.

sections.h2: What a roofer's inspection report should include
sections.body: A clear inspection report gives you and your insurer a shared record of the roof's condition. When we inspect a storm-damaged roof, we look at the whole system, not just the obvious broken pieces. A useful report typically covers:
bullets: The roof type, approximate age if known, and overall condition before the storm, where it can be judged.
Labeled photos of each area of damage, with notes on where it is on the roof.
Broken, slipped or missing tile; creased, torn or missing shingles; lifted or damaged flashing; damaged coating on flat roofs.
Signs of water getting past the top layer, such as wet or torn underlayment and stained decking.
Interior and attic observations that line up with the roof damage.
Recommended repairs or replacement, and what can wait versus what needs attention now.

sections.h2: How to spot and avoid storm chasers
sections.body: After a big monsoon, crews sometimes arrive from out of town, knock on doors and push homeowners to sign on the spot. Some do poor work and leave before problems show up. Take your time, even when water is coming in.
bullets: Look up any contractor's license on the Arizona Registrar of Contractors website before you sign anything.
Be wary of anyone who asks you to sign a contract or an assignment of your insurance benefits at the door.
Be cautious if someone offers to waive or cover your deductible; that is a red flag, and your deductible is part of your agreement with your insurer.
Ask for a local office address and phone number, and confirm they are real.
Avoid paying a large amount up front in cash.
Get the scope of work, materials and timeline in writing.

sections.body:
Some storm damage is a straightforward repair, such as replacing a handful of broken tiles. Other times the wind has damaged the underlayment across a large area, or an older roof cannot be repaired cleanly, and replacement makes more sense. A good roofer will explain the difference and show you why.

Every roof is different, so we do not quote prices without seeing it. For a general sense of what affects cost, read our Roofing Cost Guide, and see our storm damage repair and roof inspection pages for more on how we help.

faqs: Does homeowners insurance cover monsoon roof damage in Arizona?

Many policies cover sudden damage from wind, hail or falling objects, but coverage depends on your specific policy. Wear and tear, old age and long-term leaks are often excluded. Call your insurer and ask them to explain your coverage and deductible for storm damage.
Should I call my roofer or my insurance company first?

You can do both on the same day. Reporting the loss promptly to your insurer starts the claim, and a roofer's inspection gives you a clear picture of the damage. Ask your insurer whether they want a roofer's report before or after the adjuster visit.
Can I put a tarp on my roof myself?

We do not recommend it, especially on tile. Walking on tile breaks it, and ladders and wet surfaces after a storm are dangerous. Focus on protecting the inside of your home and have a roofer handle temporary protection on the roof.
How do I know if a roofer is licensed in Arizona?

Search the contractor's name or license number on the Arizona Registrar of Contractors website. The listing shows whether the license is active and the type of work it covers. Integrity Roofing's license is ROC #096629.
What if the adjuster misses some of the damage?

Read the insurer's estimate carefully and compare it with your photos and your roofer's report. If something looks missing, contact your insurer, ask how they handle a review or supplement, and send any supporting documentation they request.
How long do I have to file a roof damage claim?

Time limits vary by policy and insurer, so check your policy or ask your agent. In general, report damage as soon as you reasonably can. Waiting can make it harder to show the damage came from a specific storm.
Is a leak after a storm always storm damage?

Not always. A storm can expose an older problem, such as underlayment that was already worn out under the tile. A careful inspection helps separate new storm damage from long-term wear, which matters because insurers often treat them differently.
Do you work directly with insurance companies?

We inspect the roof, document the damage with photos and notes, and can share that report with you to provide to your insurer. Decisions about coverage are made by your insurance company. Call us at 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm, to schedule an inspection.

title: Solar Panels and Your Arizona Roof | Integrity Roofing
desc: Thinking about solar in Arizona? Learn how roof age, mounting, flashing and detach-and-reset work affect your roof, and who to call if a solar roof leaks.
h1: Solar panels and your roof: what Arizona homeowners should know
lead: Solar panels can sit on your roof for decades, so the roof under them matters. Here is how to plan solar around your roof's age, type and condition, and how to avoid leaks later.
answer: Before you install solar, have your roof inspected and make sure it has enough life left to outlast the panels, because removing and reinstalling a system later adds cost and hassle. On tile roofs the underlayment is the main concern, since it often wears out before the tile. Every bolt that goes through the roof needs proper flashing, and you should know in writing who is responsible if a mount leaks.

sections.h2: Check the roof's age and condition before you go solar
sections.body:
Solar panels are designed to last a long time. If your roof needs major work a few years after the panels go up, the system has to come off so the roof can be repaired or replaced, then go back on. Planning ahead avoids paying for that twice.

Ask a roofer to inspect the roof before you sign a solar contract. On an asphalt shingle roof, look at shingle age, granule loss and curling. On a concrete or clay tile roof, the tile itself can last a very long time, but the underlayment beneath it is what keeps water out, and in Arizona heat it often wears out well before the tile does. If the underlayment is near the end of its life, replacing it before solar goes on is usually the smarter order.

Detach and reset is the process of removing solar panels and racking, setting them aside safely, doing the roof work, and then reinstalling the system. It comes up when you re-roof, replace tile underlayment, or repair a leak under the array.

The electrical side of a solar system should be handled by a licensed solar or electrical contractor. In most cases your solar company, or a company that specializes in this work, removes and reinstalls the panels while the roofer handles the roof. We coordinate timing with your solar company so the roof is ready when they return. Ask both companies for a clear schedule, and ask the solar company whether reinstalling affects any warranty on the system.

sections.h2: Penetrations and flashing: where leaks start
sections.body: Most solar systems on sloped roofs are held down by mounts bolted through the roof into the rafters. Each of those bolts is a hole in your roof. Done well, every mount is flashed so water sheds around it. Done poorly, a mount sealed only with caulk or sealant can start leaking once the sealant dries out and cracks in the sun.
bullets: Each mount should be anchored into structure, not just the roof deck.
Mounts should have proper flashing that laps correctly with the roofing material above and below it.
Sealant can help, but it should not be the only thing keeping water out.
Wire runs and conduit that pass through the roof need their own properly flashed penetrations.
Ask your installer what mounting system they use and how they flash it on your roof type.

sections.body:
Tile roofs are common across the East Valley, and they take more care with solar. Concrete and clay tile cracks if it is stepped on the wrong way, and installers have to walk the roof to place mounts. Broken tiles under the array can go unnoticed for years.

There are a few common approaches. Tile hooks attach to the rafters and reach out between tiles so the tile can be put back. Another method removes tile at each mount location and replaces it with a flashed base. Either way, the underlayment under the tile must be protected and sealed at every penetration. After installation, it is worth having the roof checked for cracked or slipped tiles. See our tile roofs page for more on how tile roofs are built.

sections.h2: Solar on flat and foam roofs
sections.body:
Many Arizona homes, especially older ones and those with Pueblo or territorial styles, have flat or low-slope roofs. Solar on these roofs may use a tilted racking system that is either weighted down with ballast or attached through the roof.

On a spray foam roof, each attachment needs to be sealed into the foam and coating system so water cannot get into the foam. Racking should also leave room to recoat the roof, because foam roofs need periodic recoating. Heavy ballast and foot paths need to be planned so they do not crush or wear the roof surface. If your flat roof is due for a recoat or repair, do it before the panels go on.

sections.h2: Who is responsible if a solar roof leaks?
sections.body: This is one of the most common questions we hear, and the answer depends on your contracts. In general, the company that made the penetration is responsible for the leaks at that penetration, and the roofer is responsible for the roofing work they did. Warranties vary a lot, so read them before you sign.
bullets: Ask the solar company in writing whether they warrant roof penetrations and for how long.
Ask whether using a different roofer later, for repairs or detach and reset, affects that warranty.
Keep copies of your solar contract, roof warranty and any inspection photos together.
If a leak shows up under the panels, call the solar installer and a roofer so the cause can be traced.
If your solar company is no longer in business, a roofer can still find and repair the leak.

sections.h2: Critter guards keep birds and debris out
sections.body:
The gap between panels and the roof is a shaded, sheltered spot, and pigeons love it. Nesting birds leave droppings, nesting material and debris that hold moisture, clog roof valleys and can damage wiring. Critter guard is a mesh barrier installed around the edges of the array to keep animals out.

If you already have birds under your panels, the nesting material should be cleaned out before guards are installed. The mesh should attach to the panel frames, not be screwed into the roof, so it does not add new holes.

The best results come when the roof and the solar system are planned as a pair. Get the roof inspected, handle any repairs or replacement first, and share your roof's details with the solar installer. If you are not sure whether your roof is ready, call us at 602-548-3770. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. For a general sense of re-roofing costs, see our Roofing Cost Guide.

faqs: Should I replace my roof before installing solar?

If your roof is close to the end of its life, it usually makes sense to replace it, or replace tile underlayment, before solar goes on. That avoids paying to remove and reinstall the panels a few years later. An inspection will tell you how much life the roof has left.
Can solar panels be installed on a tile roof?

Yes. Installers commonly use tile hooks or replace tile at each mount with a flashed base. The key is protecting and sealing the underlayment at every penetration and replacing any tile that cracks during installation.
Do solar panels cause roof leaks?

Panels themselves do not, but the mounts and wire penetrations can if they are not flashed and sealed correctly. Most solar-related leaks we see trace back to a mount, a conduit penetration or tiles broken during installation.
Who removes my solar panels when I re-roof?

Usually your solar company or a company that specializes in detach and reset handles the panels and electrical work. The roofer does the roof work in between. We coordinate the schedule with your solar company.
Do solar panels protect my roof from the sun?

Panels do shade the part of the roof they cover, which can reduce heat and UV exposure there. The roof around the array still ages normally, and the area under the panels is harder to inspect, so it still needs attention.
How do I keep pigeons out from under my solar panels?
Have the area cleaned out and then install critter guard mesh around the array. The mesh should clip to the panel frames rather than being screwed into the roof, so it does not create new holes.
Can solar go on a foam roof?

Yes, but each attachment must be sealed into the foam and coating so water cannot get in. Plan the layout so the roof can still be recoated, and handle any needed recoat or repairs before the panels are installed.
Does Integrity Roofing install solar panels?

No. We are roofers, not solar installers. We inspect roofs before solar, repair and replace roofs under existing systems, and coordinate with your solar company when panels need to come off and go back on.

title: Attic Heat and Roof Ventilation in Arizona | Integrity Roofing
desc: How attic ventilation, cool roofs, radiant barriers and insulation work in Arizona heat, how heat ages your roof, and the signs your attic is poorly vented.
h1: Attic heat, roof ventilation and energy in Arizona
lead: In a Phoenix-area summer, the attic is often the hottest place in the house. How your roof breathes affects your cooling bills, your comfort and how long your roof lasts.
answer: A well-vented attic pulls cooler air in low at the eaves or soffits and lets hot air out high near the ridge, keeping that intake and exhaust balanced. In Arizona, good ventilation, proper insulation and a reflective roof surface work together to reduce attic heat. Less heat in the attic helps underlayment and shingles last longer and makes your air conditioner's job easier.

sections.h2: Why attic heat matters so much in Arizona
sections.body:
Arizona sun beats down on roofs for most of the year. On a summer afternoon, a dark roof surface gets far hotter than the air temperature, and that heat soaks through into the attic. In an attic with poor airflow, the heat builds hour after hour and does not fully clear out overnight.

That trapped heat pushes down through the ceiling into your living space and heats any air ducts running through the attic. It also bakes the roofing materials from below while the sun bakes them from above.

sections.h2: Intake and exhaust: how ventilation works
sections.body: Attic ventilation relies on a simple idea: hot air rises. A balanced system has two parts.
bullets: Intake vents sit low on the roof, usually in the soffits or at the eaves, and let cooler outside air in.
Exhaust vents sit high, near the ridge, and let hot air escape. Common types include ridge vents, low-profile off-ridge vents, turbine vents and gable vents.
Air should flow from the intake, across the underside of the roof deck, and out the exhaust.
Intake and exhaust should be roughly balanced. Too much exhaust and not enough intake can pull air from the wrong places, including from inside your house.
Mixing different exhaust types on the same roof can short-circuit airflow, with one vent pulling air in through another instead of from the eaves.

sections.h2: How much ventilation does a roof need?
sections.body:
Building codes set a minimum amount of net free vent area based on the size of the attic floor. A common rule of thumb is 1 square foot of ventilation for every 150 square feet of attic floor, or 1 for every 300 when the system is balanced between high and low vents and meets certain conditions. Your local code and the vent manufacturer's ratings decide the exact numbers.

When we replace a roof, we look at the existing ventilation and recommend changes if it is not enough or not balanced. Vents also have to work with the roof type; tile roofs use vents designed to sit with the tile profile, and shingle roofs commonly use ridge vents or off-ridge vents.

sections.h2: How heat ages underlayment and shingles
sections.body:
Heat and UV are the main reasons roofs wear out in Arizona. On asphalt shingle roofs, years of high heat dry out the asphalt, which can lead to curling, cracking, blistering and faster granule loss. A hot attic adds heat from underneath, which can shorten shingle life further.

On tile roofs, the tile is durable, but the underlayment beneath it is what actually keeps water out. Traditional felt underlayment gets brittle as it bakes year after year and eventually cracks, especially at the eaves, valleys and around penetrations. That is why tile roofs in the Valley often need the underlayment replaced, a job called a re-felt or lift and relay, long before the tile itself is worn out.

A cool roof is designed to reflect more sunlight and release absorbed heat more easily than a standard roof. Lighter colors and specially rated materials stay noticeably cooler in direct sun. The Cool Roof Rating Council publishes independent ratings for solar reflectance and thermal emittance that let you compare products.

On flat roofs, a white elastomeric coating or a coated spray foam roof is one of the most effective ways to reduce heat. On sloped roofs, lighter tile or shingle colors help, though color choices may be limited by your HOA. Keep in mind that coatings get dirty and wear over time, and a dirty or worn coating reflects less.

A radiant barrier is a reflective material, often foil-faced sheathing or a foil sheet stapled to the underside of the rafters, that reduces the amount of heat radiating from the hot roof deck down into the attic. Radiant barriers tend to work best in hot, sunny climates like ours, and the U.S. Department of Energy notes they can be especially helpful when ducts run through the attic.

For a radiant barrier to work, the shiny side needs an air space facing it, and it should not be laid directly on top of attic insulation where dust will collect and reduce its effect. It does not replace ventilation or insulation; it works alongside them.

Ventilation moves heat out of the attic. Insulation slows heat from moving through the ceiling into your home. You need both. Insulation is rated by R-value; the higher the number, the more it resists heat flow. The Department of Energy's Energy Saver site lists recommended attic R-values by climate zone, and it is a good place to check what fits the Phoenix area.
bullets: Insulation should be spread evenly, without bare spots or thin areas near the eaves.
Insulation should not block soffit vents. Baffles keep a clear air channel at the eaves.
Compressed, wet or rodent-damaged insulation loses much of its value and should be replaced.
Sealing gaps around light fixtures, attic hatches and plumbing keeps conditioned air out of the attic.

sections.h2: Signs your attic is poorly ventilated
sections.body: Many ventilation problems are easy to spot once you know what to look for. Some signs show up inside the house, and some on the roof.
bullets: Upstairs rooms that stay much hotter than the rest of the house.
An attic that feels like an oven even in the early morning.
Soffit vents that are painted over, blocked by insulation or missing.
Shingles that are curling, blistering or losing granules faster than expected.
Brittle, cracked underlayment visible at the eaves of a tile roof.
Signs of condensation, such as rusty nail tips or stains on the underside of the roof deck, which can happen in winter or monsoon humidity.

sections.body: If your attic runs hot or your roof is aging faster than it should, a roof inspection can check vents, underlayment and roof surface together. Call us at 602-548-3770. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. If a new roof is on the table, our Roofing Cost Guide explains what affects the price.

faqs: What is the difference between intake and exhaust vents?

Intake vents sit low, usually in the soffits or eaves, and let outside air into the attic. Exhaust vents sit high near the ridge and let hot air out. A good system has both, roughly balanced, so air moves steadily across the underside of the roof.
Can I have too much attic ventilation?

It is possible to have the wrong kind. Adding lots of exhaust without enough intake, or mixing exhaust types, can pull air from inside your home or from one vent into another. Balance matters more than simply adding more vents.
Does a lighter roof color really make a difference in Arizona?
Yes. Lighter, more reflective surfaces absorb less sun and stay cooler than dark ones, which can reduce attic heat. On sloped roofs, check your HOA's approved colors before choosing.
Are radiant barriers worth it in Phoenix?

Radiant barriers are most effective in hot, sunny climates and when ducts run through the attic, which describes many Valley homes. They work best alongside good ventilation and insulation, not as a substitute for either.
Should attic fans be used in Arizona?

Powered attic fans can help in some homes, but they can also pull cooled air out of the house through ceiling gaps if the attic does not have enough intake. Have the whole system evaluated before adding one.
Why does my tile roof need new underlayment if the tiles look fine?

In Arizona heat, the underlayment under the tile often wears out long before the tile does. Once it cracks, water that gets past the tile can reach the deck. Replacing it while reusing good tile is called a re-felt or lift and relay.
Does a new roof fix ventilation problems?
It is the best time to fix them. During a replacement, vents can be added, removed or rebalanced to suit the roof and attic. We review ventilation as part of every replacement.
How can I tell if my attic insulation is enough?

Look for even coverage with no bare spots, and measure the depth in a few places. Compare it with the recommended R-values for our climate on the Department of Energy's Energy Saver site, or ask an insulation contractor to check.

title: Caring for Flat and Foam Roofs in Arizona | Integrity Roofing
desc: Keep your Arizona flat or spray foam roof healthy: manage ponding, clear drains and scuppers, check parapets, time recoats, and handle blisters and bird damage.
h1: Caring for flat and foam roofs in Arizona
lead: Flat and low-slope roofs are common across the Valley, from older ranch homes to Pueblo-style houses and commercial buildings. A little regular care keeps them watertight and helps them last.
answer: Flat and foam roofs last longest when water drains off quickly, drains and scuppers stay clear, and the protective coating is renewed before it wears through. Check the roof after monsoon storms and at least once a year, watch for ponding, blisters, cracks and bird damage, and keep foot traffic to a minimum. Recoating a foam roof on time is far easier than repairing foam that has been exposed to the sun.

sections.h2: How flat and foam roofs are built
sections.body:
Flat roofs are not perfectly flat; they have a slight slope so water can drain toward drains, scuppers or gutters. Common flat roof systems in Arizona include built-up roofs, modified bitumen, single-ply membranes and spray polyurethane foam, often called SPF or foam.

A foam roof is sprayed on as a liquid that expands into a seamless, insulating layer, then covered with a protective coating. The foam provides insulation and the waterproof body of the roof, but it breaks down quickly in UV light. The coating is what protects it, which is why coating care is the heart of foam roof maintenance. See our flat roofing page for more on each system.

Ponding is water that stays on the roof after a storm instead of draining away. A common industry guideline treats water that remains 48 hours after rain as ponding. In Arizona sun, small puddles often evaporate quickly, but repeated ponding in the same spot can wear coatings faster, collect dirt and debris, and add weight.

Ponding usually points to a low spot, a clogged drain or a roof that has settled. Small areas can sometimes be built up with additional foam or other material during a repair or recoat. Larger or deeper ponding areas should be looked at by a roofer to find the cause.

Water leaves most flat roofs through roof drains, scuppers (openings through the parapet wall) or canales, the decorative channels common on Pueblo-style homes. When these clog, water backs up and finds other ways into the building.
bullets: Check drains and scuppers before monsoon season starts on June 15 and after major storms.
Remove leaves, dirt, tennis balls, nesting material and other debris.
Look for cracks or gaps where the scupper or drain meets the roof surface.
Make sure water exiting a scupper or canale is directed away from walls and the foundation.
Keep tree branches trimmed back so leaves do not collect on the roof.

sections.body:
Parapets are the short walls that extend above the roof line on many flat-roof homes. They hide equipment and give homes their classic Southwest look, but they are a common source of leaks. Water can get in through cracked stucco on top of the wall, through gaps where the wall meets the roof, or through damaged parapet caps.

When you inspect, look at the tops of parapets for cracks and at the inside corners where the roof turns up the wall. On foam roofs, the foam and coating usually run up the inside of the parapet, and that transition should be smooth and intact. Stucco repair on the outside of a parapet may need a stucco contractor, while the roof side is roofer territory.

Coatings on foam and other flat roofs slowly wear away from sun, heat, weather and dirt. As the coating thins, it reflects less heat and protects less. Eventually the foam underneath shows through, often with a tan or orange color, and once foam is exposed to UV it starts to break down.

How often a roof needs a recoat depends on the coating type, how thick it was applied and how the roof is used. Many foam roofs are recoated every several years, and your roofer can give you a timeline for your specific system. The key is to recoat while the foam is still healthy. A timely recoat with an elastomeric coating is far less work than tearing out damaged foam.
bullets: Chalky residue that rubs off on your hand is normal aging, but heavy chalking means the coating is thinning.
Cracking or peeling coating should be repaired before water gets underneath.
Any exposed foam should be covered as soon as practical.
Annual checks make it easier to plan a recoat before damage starts.

sections.body:
Blisters are raised, bubble-like areas in a roof surface. On foam roofs, blisters can form when moisture gets trapped or when the foam or coating loses its bond. On built-up and other membrane roofs, trapped air or moisture between layers can cause similar bubbles.

Small, stable blisters are not always an emergency, but they should not be ignored. If a blister cracks or is punctured, water can get in. A roofer can cut out the damaged area, let it dry if needed, and fill and recoat it. Do not cut blisters open yourself.

Birds sometimes peck at foam roofs, leaving small holes or gouges. The soft foam under the coating is easy for them to dig into. Each hole is a place where water and UV can reach the foam.

Look for small pockmarks, especially near parapets, AC units and other spots where birds perch. Small holes can be filled and coated during routine maintenance. Hail and wind-blown debris during monsoon storms can also leave dents and punctures that should be sealed.

sections.h2: Foot traffic and rooftop HVAC units
sections.body: Many Arizona flat roofs carry air conditioning units, evaporative coolers, solar panels and vents. Each one brings service visits, and service visits bring foot traffic. Repeated walking wears through coatings, and dropped tools or screws can puncture the surface.
bullets: Ask HVAC technicians to stay on established paths and avoid dragging equipment.
Walk pads can protect high-traffic routes to equipment.
Check around HVAC units after service for screws, panels or debris left behind.
Look at the curbs and stands that support equipment, and at the seals around ductwork and electrical lines.
Evaporative coolers can drip or overflow; a leaking cooler can damage the roof over time.

sections.body: Call for help if you see exposed foam, standing water that does not drain, cracked coating, blisters, stains on ceilings below a flat roof, or damage after a storm. We handle repairs and maintenance, recoats and replacements on flat and foam roofs. Call us at 602-548-3770. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. For a general idea of what affects pricing, see our Roofing Cost Guide.

faqs: How often should a foam roof be recoated?

It depends on the coating type, its thickness and how the roof is used. Many foam roofs are recoated every several years. An inspection can tell you how much coating is left and when to plan the next recoat.
What does it mean if I can see orange or tan foam?
It usually means the protective coating has worn through and the foam is exposed. UV light breaks down exposed foam, so the area should be repaired and recoated as soon as practical.
Is a little standing water on my flat roof a problem?
Small puddles that dry within a day or two are common. Water that stays longer, or ponds in the same spot after every storm, can wear the roof faster and should be looked at to find the cause.
Can a foam roof be repaired, or does it need to be replaced?

Many foam roofs can be repaired and recoated as long as the foam is mostly dry and in good shape. If large areas are wet or badly damaged, those areas or the whole roof may need to be removed and replaced.
Why are there small holes in my foam roof?

Birds pecking at the foam are a common cause, especially near parapets and rooftop equipment. Hail and debris can also cause punctures. Small holes can be filled and coated during routine maintenance.
How do I keep HVAC technicians from damaging my roof?
Ask them to use a set path, avoid dragging equipment and remove all screws and debris when they finish. Walk pads along common routes help protect the coating.
Should I clean my flat roof drains myself?

If you can safely reach the roof with a secure ladder and the roof is cool and dry, clearing loose debris from drains and scuppers is reasonable. If access is difficult or you are unsure, have a professional handle it.
Do flat roofs leak more than sloped roofs?
Not necessarily. A well-maintained flat roof with good drainage can perform very well. Flat roofs do depend more on clear drains and a healthy coating or membrane, so regular checks matter.

title: HOA Roof Approval Guide for the East Valley | Integrity Roofing
desc: Re-roofing in an East Valley HOA? Learn how architectural review works, what to send, matching tile profile and color, typical timelines and permit basics.
h1: HOA approval for a re-roof in the East Valley
lead: Many neighborhoods in Gilbert, Mesa, Chandler, Queen Creek and San Tan Valley have homeowners associations with rules about how roofs look. Getting approval before work starts keeps your project on track.
answer: Most HOAs require architectural review approval before you replace a roof or change its color, tile profile or material. You typically send the HOA's request with the product name, color, profile and a sample or photo, then wait for a written approval before work starts. Rules and timelines differ by community, so read your HOA's guidelines and check with your city about building permits.

sections.body:
Roofs are one of the most visible parts of a home, and HOAs use design guidelines to keep a consistent look across the neighborhood. Many communities in the East Valley were built with concrete tile roofs in a set of colors chosen by the builder, and the HOA's guidelines often aim to keep that look as homes are re-roofed.

Every HOA is different. Some have a short list of approved roof colors and materials, others allow anything that matches the home's style, and some require approval only when you change the look. Your HOA's CC&Rs and architectural guidelines are the place to start.
Before you pick a tile or shingle, get the current documents from your HOA or its management company. They are often available through the community's website or resident portal.
bullets: The CC&Rs, which set out the community's restrictions.
The architectural or design guidelines, which usually cover roof materials, colors and profiles.
The architectural review request document and any instructions for completing it.
Any approved color palette or list of pre-approved roofing products.
Meeting schedules for the architectural review committee, if it meets on set dates.

sections.body: Many HOAs require approval for any exterior change, including a full re-roof, even if you plan to use the same material and color. Others only require it if something visible changes. Common situations that usually need approval include:
bullets: Replacing the roof with a different tile color, blend or profile.
Switching from tile to shingles, or the other way around, where the guidelines allow it.
Changing gutter, fascia or trim colors as part of the project.
Adding new visible items, such as roof vents in a different color or solar panels.

sections.body:
Concrete tile comes in several profiles, which describe the shape of each tile. Common ones include flat, low-profile S and high-profile S (often called Spanish or mission style). Colors range from single solid tones to blends of several shades. Your HOA may require the same profile and a similar color to the original, or a choice from an approved palette.

Exact matches can be hard, especially on older homes. Tile colors fade over time, and some original colors are no longer made. If you are only replacing underlayment through a re-felt or lift and relay, most of the existing tile is reused, so the look rarely changes, though a few replacement tiles may be needed. If a full tile replacement is planned, ask your roofer to bring samples so you can compare them with your home and your neighbors' roofs. Learn more on our tile roofs page.

sections.h2: What to include in an architectural review request
sections.body: A complete request is the fastest way to get approval. Incomplete requests are often sent back, which restarts the clock. Most HOAs ask for some combination of the following:
bullets: Your name, address and lot number, and the HOA's request document, completed in full.
The roofing manufacturer, product line, color name and profile.
A product brochure, color sheet or photo of the tile or shingle, and sometimes a physical sample.
A photo of your home as it is now.
The contractor's name and Arizona ROC license number. Ours is ROC #096629.
Notes on any other visible changes, such as vents, gutters or fascia color.
Your planned start date, if the HOA asks for one.

sections.body:
Review times vary widely. Some HOAs approve standard requests within days, while others only review at monthly committee meetings. Many guidelines state a maximum review period, so check yours. Plan ahead and send your request well before you hope to start, especially if you want the work done before monsoon season begins on June 15.

Wait for written approval before work begins. Starting without approval can lead to fines or a requirement to change the roof, and that is an expensive mistake. Keep a copy of the approval letter with your roofing contract and warranty paperwork.

HOA approval and a building permit are two different things. The HOA controls appearance in the community. The city or town controls building safety and code compliance. Whether a re-roof needs a permit, and what the permit requires, depends on your city and the scope of work.

Requirements differ between Gilbert, Mesa, Chandler, Queen Creek and other cities, and can also vary based on whether the roof deck or structure is changed. Check your city's building department website or call them for current rules. On jobs that require a permit, the roofing contractor typically pulls it; ask your roofer to confirm.

sections.h2: How we help with HOA projects
sections.body: We work in HOA communities across the East Valley. We can provide product information, color names, sample tiles and our license details for your request, and we schedule work after you have approval. See our pages on roof replacement and roofing in Gilbert, and our Roofing Cost Guide for what affects price. To get started, call 602-548-3770. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

faqs: Do I need HOA approval to replace my roof with the same tile?

Many HOAs still require approval for a full re-roof, even with the same material and color. Others only require it if something visible changes. Check your architectural guidelines or ask your management company.
Do I need HOA approval for a re-felt or lift and relay?

Often not, since the existing tile is put back and the look does not change, but some HOAs want to be notified of any roof work. If replacement tiles will be noticeably different, ask before work starts.
What if my original tile color is no longer made?

This is common on older homes. Your roofer can bring samples of current colors that come close, and you can include them in your request. Some HOAs have an approved palette that lists acceptable replacements.
How long does HOA roof approval take?
It depends on the HOA. Some respond within days, while others review requests only at scheduled committee meetings. Your guidelines may list a maximum review time, so plan ahead.
Can my HOA make me use a specific roofing contractor?
HOAs typically regulate how a roof looks, not who installs it, though some have requirements such as licensing and insurance. Read your CC&Rs and guidelines or ask your management company.
Is a building permit required for a re-roof?

It depends on your city and the scope of the work. Rules differ between Gilbert, Mesa, Chandler and other cities. Check with your city's building department, and ask your roofer whether they will pull any permit required.
What happens if I re-roof without HOA approval?
Your HOA may issue a violation, charge fines or require changes if the roof does not meet the guidelines. Waiting for written approval avoids that risk.
Can I switch from tile to shingles in an HOA?
Some HOAs allow it and many do not, depending on the community's design standards. Check the architectural guidelines first, and include product details in your request if it is allowed.

title: Safe DIY Roof Checks for Arizona Homes | Integrity Roofing
desc: Check your roof safely from the ground and attic: what to spot with binoculars and a flashlight, ceiling stain clues, what not to do, and when to call a pro.
h1: Safe DIY roof checks from the ground and the attic
lead: You can learn a lot about your roof without ever climbing onto it. These checks help you spot problems early and know when it is time to call a roofer.
answer: Homeowners can safely check a roof from the ground with binoculars and from the attic with a flashlight, looking for missing or broken tile, lifted shingles, damaged flashing, daylight, water stains and wet insulation. Do not walk on a tile roof and avoid climbing onto any roof, especially in Arizona heat. If you find stains, leaks or damage, call a licensed roofer.

sections.body: Falls from ladders and roofs cause serious injuries every year. Roofing crews use training and safety equipment for a reason. On top of the fall risk, Arizona roofs add a few hazards of their own.
bullets: Tile breaks. Concrete and clay tile cracks when stepped on in the wrong spot, and a broken tile can lead to a leak.
Heat. Roof surfaces in summer can get hot enough to burn skin, and heat exhaustion can set in quickly.
Slick surfaces. Loose granules, dust, dew and monsoon rain make roofs slippery.
Hidden damage. A weak or rotted deck may not hold your weight.

sections.body:
Pick a dry, calm day. In summer, do outdoor checks early in the morning when the light is good and temperatures are lower. Twice a year is a good habit, once before monsoon season starts on June 15 and once in the fall, plus a quick look after any big storm.

Bring binoculars or a phone with a good zoom, a notepad and a flashlight for the attic. Take photos each time so you can compare from year to year and show a roofer exactly what you saw.

sections.h2: What to look for from the ground
sections.body: Walk all the way around the house and look at each roof slope. Step back far enough to see the upper areas, and check from across the street if you have a two-story home.
bullets: Missing, cracked or slipped tiles, especially along ridges, hips and edges.
Shingles that are missing, curling, creased or lifted, or patches of darker color where granules have worn away.
Granules collecting in gutters or at downspout outlets.
Bent, loose or missing flashing around chimneys, walls, vents and skylights.
Damaged or missing roof vents and pipe boots.
Sagging areas or a ridge line that is not straight.
Peeling fascia paint or stained soffits, which can signal water at the roof edge.
Birds, pigeons or debris under solar panels.

sections.h2: Check the attic with a flashlight
sections.body:
The attic shows you the underside of the roof, which is often where leaks show up first. In summer, Arizona attics can get dangerously hot, so go in the early morning or wait for a cooler month. Tell someone you are going up, and limit your time.

Step only on joists or a floored walkway. The drywall between joists will not hold you, and a misstep can put a foot through the ceiling. Watch for nails sticking through the roof deck overhead, and wear a mask, gloves and long sleeves around insulation.
bullets: Water stains, dark spots or streaks on the underside of the roof deck and rafters.
Wet, matted or discolored insulation.
Daylight coming through the deck, other than at designed vents.
Signs of pests, such as droppings or chewed insulation.
Soffit vents blocked by insulation.
Damp areas around plumbing vents, exhaust fans and chimneys.

sections.h2: What ceiling stains can tell you
sections.body:
A ceiling stain is often the first sign a roof is leaking, but it does not always sit directly under the problem. Water can travel along rafters, the underlayment or the top of drywall before it shows up. A stain near an exterior wall may point to flashing or an edge problem, while a stain near a bathroom may be plumbing or an exhaust fan instead of the roof.

Watch whether the stain grows after rain. A stain that only appears after storms usually means a roof leak. A stain that grows when it has not rained may be plumbing, an AC drain line or condensation. Take a photo and mark the edge of the stain with pencil so you can tell if it spreads.

If you have gutters or a flat roof with scuppers, clear drainage matters before monsoon season. If you use a ladder, set it on firm, level ground, extend it at least 3 feet above the edge you are working at and keep three points of contact. Have someone hold the ladder.

Never lean a ladder against a gutter that is loose, and do not step from the ladder onto a tile roof. If you cannot reach something safely from the ladder, leave it for a pro.

• Do not walk on tile roofs; even a careful step can crack tiles.
  • Do not go on any roof during or right after a storm, or in high heat.
  • Do not pressure wash a roof; it can strip shingle granules, damage coatings and force water under tile.
  • Do not seal over a leak with caulk or roofing cement from the top; this often traps water and hides the real source.
  • Do not cut open blisters on flat or foam roofs.
  • Do not work near overhead power lines or solar wiring.

Call a licensed roofer if you see active leaks, ceiling stains, wet insulation, missing or broken tile, damaged flashing, exposed foam on a flat roof or anything you are unsure about. A professional roof inspection covers areas you cannot see from the ground, including underlayment and flashing under the tile. For repairs, see repairs and maintenance.

Call us at 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours. Every roof is different; our Roofing Cost Guide explains what affects the cost of repairs and replacement.

faqs: How often should I check my roof myself?
Twice a year is a good routine, once before monsoon season and once in the fall. Also take a quick look from the ground after any major storm.
Can I walk on my tile roof if I am careful?

We recommend you do not. Concrete and clay tile can crack even under careful steps, and a cracked tile can let water reach the underlayment. Roofers know where to step and still sometimes need to replace tile.
Is it safe to go in my attic in summer?
Arizona attics can get extremely hot in summer, which can lead to heat exhaustion quickly. Go early in the morning or wait for cooler months, limit your time and tell someone you are up there.
What does daylight in my attic mean?
Light at designed vents is normal. Light coming through the roof deck itself can mean a hole or gap that water could also get through, and it should be checked by a roofer.
How do I know if a ceiling stain is from the roof?

If it appears or grows after rain, a roof leak is likely. If it changes when it has not rained, plumbing, an AC drain line or condensation may be the cause. A roofer can trace the source from the attic and roof.
What do binoculars help me see?
Binoculars let you spot broken or slipped tile, lifted shingles, damaged flashing and worn vents from the safety of the ground. Taking photos through a phone zoom works too and gives you a record.
Should I use roof sealant to fix a small leak?

We do not recommend it. Sealant on top of the roof often traps water or sends it somewhere else, and it makes the real problem harder to find. It is better to have the source found and repaired properly.
What should I tell a roofer when I call?
Describe where the stain or damage is, when you first noticed it and whether it changes after rain. Photos from the ground and attic are very helpful.
